description: A bearing with no contact: compressed air is fed through tiny holes or a porous face into a gap a few thousandths of a millimetre thick (air bearings) or under a flexible ring-shaped bag (air casters), and the pressure of the escaping air carries the load, so parts slide or turn with no stick-slip and no wear, and tonnes can be pushed across a smooth floor by hand.

title: Centrifugal pump
description: A motor spins a wheel of curved blades (the impeller) inside a spiral casing (the volute); water entering at the centre is whirled outwards, gains speed and pressure, and leaves through the outlet, giving a large, smooth flow at fairly low pressure, as long as the pump is already full of water (Wikipedia 'Centrifugal pump').

title: Automatic siphon
description: A capped tube (the bell) sits over a standpipe that drains a tank; when the rising water spills into the standpipe it pulls the air out of the bell and starts a siphon that empties the tank much faster than it fills, until air rushes in under the bell's rim and breaks the siphon, so a steady trickle in becomes a regular flood-and-drain cycle with no moving parts or timer (University of Hawai'i CTAHR BIO-10; FAO 2014).

title: Soldered wire joint
description: Stripped wire ends are twisted, hooked or laid side by side, molten solder is flowed into them with a soldering iron so it bonds to the copper, and the finished joint is covered with heat-shrink tubing; it is the basic permanent wire joint that crimps, solder sleeves, lever connectors and wire nuts are compared with.

title: Wood screw
description: A sharp, coarse-threaded screw that forms its own thread in wood or board and clamps the parts together under its head; with the right pilot and clearance holes it is the everyday way to fix wood to wood, and the coach screw (big, hex-headed) and Confirmat screw (fat, for chipboard furniture) are its heavy and flat-pack versions.

title: Basic knots
description: Three knots built from the same single tuck: the overhand makes a lump in the end of a cord so it can't slip through a hole, the half hitch ties a cord round a post or ring, and the reef knot ties the two ends of one cord round a bundle, with a slipped version that becomes the shoelace bow; they are the baseline that better knots for each job are compared with.

title: Shims, spacers and standoffs
description: A shim, spacer or standoff is a piece of known thickness or length put between two parts, so that the gap, height or spacing between them is set by that piece and then held when the parts are bolted or pressed together.

title: Welded metal joint
description: Welding melts the edges of two metal parts, usually with extra filler metal from a wire or rod, using an electric arc or a gas flame, so the melted metal flows together and cools into one continuous piece: the strongest permanent way to join metal parts of the same or compatible metals.

title: Battery holder and battery contacts
description: A battery holder grips one or more cells and connects them through springy metal contacts pressed against their ends (and, for several cells, links them in series or parallel), so the cells can be taken out and replaced by hand while the device stays wired to the holder.

title: Pogo pin
description: A spring-loaded plunger in a small tube that is pressed onto a flat metal pad to carry electricity between two parts that just touch, so devices can be docked, charged, tested or programmed without a plug.

title: Magnetic connector
description: Two connector halves with magnets that pull them together and line them up, so spring-loaded pins on one half press onto flat pads on the other to carry power or data, and the halves separate cleanly when pulled too hard.

title: Screw-in threaded insert
description: A threaded sleeve or a diamond-section wire coil that is screwed into a drilled or tapped hole to give soft, brittle or worn material a strong, reusable machine-screw thread.

title: Sew-on part
description: Holes, loops, slots or a thin flange designed into a rigid part let you sew it to fabric with needle and thread, so the thread loops lock the part on by shape, like a sew-on button, and it can be cut off and re-sewn later.

title: Stopper knots and cord-end anchors
description: A knot, bead or crimped sleeve that is too big to fit through a hole, or a clamp or a few turns round a post that grips the cord, holds the end of a cord, string, elastic or thin cable in a part so it can be pulled without coming out.

title: Printing onto fabric
description: A thin open mesh fabric is laid over the first few printed layers during a pause, and the rest of the print fuses through its holes, so the fabric is locked inside each printed piece and the bare fabric between pieces works as a flexible hinge.

title: Locking adjustment screws
description: Two or three screws, each opposed by a second screw, a spring or a lock nut, that set the tilt, height or end position of a plate or part and then clamp it at that exact setting, as on telescope mirror cells, 3D-printer beds and machine end stops.

title: Ball caster
description: A large ball held in a cup on small bearing balls or rollers, giving a support point that rolls equally easily in every direction, used as a small robot's third wheel or, ball-up, as the rolling surface of transfer tables and conveyors.

title: Cable through a hinge
description: A planned route for wires, flat cables or tubes across a hinge or a joint that turns less than a full turn (or a few turns), either through a hollow pin or shaft on the turning axis so the cable only twists, or as a loose loop or wound flat cable that rolls instead of kinking, with clamps on each side so the flexing happens only where it is designed to.

title: Expanding internal grip

title: Printed chainmail and tile fabric
description: A flat sheet of small tiles or rings printed in one go with each piece already looped through its neighbours, so the stiff pieces together behave like a flexible cloth for costumes, covers, bags and fidget toys, although it is not real armour.

title: Strut hub

title: Friction-welded plastic
description: Friction welding melts plastic by rubbing instead of by heating: a short length of filament spun in a rotary tool is run along a seam like a melting filler rod, or one round part is spun against another on a drill press or lathe, until the contact melts and the parts fuse into a single piece.

title: Heat-sealed seam
description: A heat-sealed seam joins two thin layers of thermoplastic film, or coating-to-coating on plastic-coated fabric, by pressing them with a hot bar, iron, wire or tip until the facing plastic melts together, giving an airtight, waterproof line with no stitches or glue: the joint behind plastic bags, inflatables, dry bags and soft-robot air pouches.

title: Tensegrity
description: A structure in which rigid struts (or two rigid halves) never touch each other and are held in a fixed shape only by tensioned cords, cables or chains, giving the 'floating' look of tensegrity tables, shelves and sculptures.

title: Wire-to-board plug connectors
description: A plastic plug (housing) holding small sprung metal sockets that have been crimped onto wire ends pushes onto a matching row of pins (header) soldered to a circuit board, making a removable, often latched and polarised, low-current connection.

title: Crimp terminals
description: A metal terminal whose barrel is squeezed (crimped) onto a stripped wire end with a crimping tool, giving a ring or fork to clamp under a screw or stud, or a blade or receptacle that pushes onto a matching tab, so a wire can be fixed to a terminal or unplugged without soldering.

title: Crimped butt splice
description: A crimped butt splice joins two wires end to end: each stripped end goes into one half of a short metal tube, a ratcheting crimp tool squeezes the tube so hard that metal and strands cold-weld into a gas-tight joint, and the plastic or glue-lined heat-shrink sleeve outside insulates it (and, for the glue-lined kind, seals it against water).

title: Spring-clamp wire connector
description: A spring-clamp wire connector joins wires, or lands them on a board or terminal block, with a pre-loaded spring instead of a screw: each stripped wire has its own spring clamp, opened by a lever or button or simply pushed past by a stiff wire, which presses it onto a tinned copper bar with the same force every time, so the joint needs no tool, never needs tightening and can be undone and reused.

title: Screw terminal
description: A screw terminal holds a stripped wire (or a crimped ring, fork or ferrule) by tightening a screw onto it, either under the screw head, under a clamping plate or with a set screw in a metal tube; it is the cheap, reusable way to land wires on boards, power supplies, barrier strips and connector strips and to undo them later with a screwdriver.

title: Wire-end ferrule
description: A thin tin-plated copper tube, usually with a colour-coded plastic collar, is slid over the stripped end of a stranded wire and crushed onto it with a crimping tool, so the strands stay together and the wire end goes into a screw or spring terminal like a single solid pin, giving a cooler, more reliable joint than bare splayed strands.

title: High-current battery plug
description: A two-pin plug and socket with thick metal contacts in a shaped housing that fits only one way round, soldered (or crimped) onto heavy wires so a battery pack can be plugged into a model, robot or charger and unplugged by hand, carrying tens of amps; the plug and the wire must both suit the current.

title: Heat-shrink tubing
description: A tube of specially treated plastic is slid over a wire or joint and heated with a hot-air gun, so it shrinks to between a half and a sixth of its diameter and grips tightly, insulating the joint and protecting it from rubbing, while glue-lined versions also melt their inner glue to seal out water.

title: Solder sleeve

title: Standard plug-and-socket connector
description: A bought plug and socket made to a published standard (USB, barrel jack, audio jack, RJ45 and many more), so a project can take power or signals from leads and chargers that already exist and be unplugged by hand; you choose by what the other device has, how often it will be plugged in, and whether it must latch or seal.

title: Insulation-displacement connector
description: Insulated wires are pushed or squeezed into slotted metal blades that cut through the insulation and grip the copper, making a gas-tight, unstripped joint; used to terminate many ribbon-cable wires in one press, punch network and phone wires into blocks and jacks, crimp RJ45 plugs, and tap a branch wire onto an existing one.

title: Binding post and banana plug
description: A binding post is a threaded metal post with a screw-down insulated cap that clamps a bare wire, spade or pin, and also takes a springy banana plug pushed into its end, so test leads and wires can be connected and removed by hand in seconds; crocodile clips and test hooks do the same job by gripping any bare wire, lead or terminal with a spring.

title: Twist-on wire connector
description: A twist-on wire connector is an insulating cap with a tapered coil spring inside that is screwed by hand onto the stripped ends of several wires, drawing them together and squeezing them into one electrical joint while covering the bare metal.

title: Conductive thread
description: Conductive thread is sewing thread made from stainless-steel fibres or silver-plated filaments that is stitched through the holes (sew tabs) of sewable boards, LEDs and battery holders, so the tight loops make the electrical contacts and the lines of stitching act as bare wires across the fabric.

title: Conductive tape
description: Conductive tape is a thin copper foil or metal-plated fabric with a peel-off sticky back, laid down as flat 'wires' on paper, card, fabric or a 3D print so that LEDs, batteries and other small parts can be taped, soldered, glued or sewn onto it; the same copper tape is used to line boxes and guitar cavities as an electrical shield.

title: Conductive glue, paint and ink
description: Conductive glue, paint and ink are adhesives, paints and inks loaded with silver, copper, nickel or carbon particles that touch each other once dry or cured, so they stick a part on or draw a track that carries a small current where solder can't be used, such as on heat-sensitive parts, glass, paper, fabric or 3D prints.

title: Flat flexible cable and latching connector
description: A flat flexible cable is a thin plastic film with many flat copper conductors whose stiffened, bared ends slide into low-profile board connectors that are clamped shut by a small latch (a ZIF connector), carrying many low-current signals between boards, cameras and displays and through hinges and moving parts.

title: Wire wrap
description: Wire wrap joins a thin solid wire to a square metal post by winding the bared wire tightly round it with a small spinning tool: the post's sharp corners bite into the wire at every turn, making about 28 tiny gas-tight, cold-welded contact points that need no solder and can be unwound and redone.

title: Hose clamp
description: A hose clamp is a ring of metal band, wire or spring steel that is tightened round the end of a hose pushed over a spigot, barb or pipe, squeezing the hose so it seals and so it can't slide off; worm-drive types tighten with a screw and can be undone, ear clamps are crimped shut once, and spring clamps hold by their own springiness.

title: Drive-in fixing pins
description: A drive-in fixing pin is a short metal pin driven into a hole that passes through two parts, locking them together so they can't rotate or slide; spring pins (slotted roll pins and coiled pins) grip by springing outwards against the hole, while solid dowel, grooved, knurled and taper pins grip by a tight or wedging fit.

title: Wall plug
description: A wall plug is a plastic (once fibre or wood) sleeve that you push into a hole drilled in brick, block, stone or concrete; driving a screw into it spreads the sleeve against the hole so the screw can hold a shelf, bracket or cabinet, and bigger metal or resin anchors do the same job for heavy loads.

title: Hollow-wall anchors
description: A hollow-wall anchor gives a screw something to hold on to in plasterboard, hollow doors and panels, either by opening out behind the board (toggles, mollies, winged anchors) or by cutting a coarse thread into it (self-drilling anchors), because a plain screw or wall plug would pull straight out of the thin, soft board.

title: Push-on edge trim
description: Push-on edge trim is a flexible U-shaped strip, usually PVC or rubber with a springy metal core, that is pressed onto a sheet or panel edge and grips it by spring force and barbed tongues, covering sharp edges, protecting cables in cut-outs (grommet edging) and, with a bulb attached, sealing doors and lids.

title: Metal brackets and plates
description: A stamped steel bracket, strap or flat plate fixed across a joint with screws, nails or teeth so that the metal carries the load the joint itself can't, from a small corner brace that stiffens a wobbly frame to a joist hanger or truss plate that holds up a floor or roof.

title: Nails, brads and tacks
description: A pointed steel pin hammered or fired into wood, where the squashed wood fibres grip its shank by friction, used to fix wood to wood (and thin board, felt, fabric or leather to wood) quickly and cheaply; it carries sideways (shear) loads well but pulls out more easily than a screw unless it has rings or a twist, is driven at an angle, or is bent over (clinched).

title: Threaded rod and studs
description: A rod threaded along its length (or at both ends) that, with nuts and washers, makes a bolt of any length, a tie rod that pulls parts together, a frame member, an axle or an adjustable spacer; a stud screws into a tapped hole and stays there so a part can be clamped over it with a nut, and a hanger bolt does the same job in wood.

title: Eye bolts, screw eyes and hooks
description: A screw or bolt that ends in a closed loop (eye) or an open hook, fixed into wood, masonry or a tapped hole to give a rope, wire, spring, chain or hanging object a fixed point to attach to; bent-wire eyes and hooks are for light loads only, while forged, shouldered and marked lifting eyes carry heavy, angled pulls.

title: Staples for wood and fabric
description: A U-shaped wire fastener driven straight into wood (or a similar soft base) by a staple gun or hammer tacker, whose flat top (crown) bridges over whatever it holds, which makes it the quick way to fix fabric, leather, mesh, plastic film, insulation and low-voltage cables flat onto wood.

title: Shackle and quick link
description: A closed metal link (a U-shaped shackle shut by a screw pin or bolt, or an oval quick link shut by a threaded sleeve) that joins rope eyes, chain, slings, straps and anchor points; because it closes completely it can't shake off like a hook, and a rated, marked one carries very heavy in-line loads.

title: Tamper-resistant fasteners
description: A screw, bolt or nut with an unusual drive (a pin in the socket, odd lobes, two holes, an odd number of sides), a slot that only grips one way, or a head that snaps off when tight, so that ordinary tools can't undo it and casual tampering with covers, battery boxes, signs and public fittings is stopped or slowed.

title: Wire-rope terminations
description: A way of finishing steel wire rope with a loop (usually wrapped round a grooved thimble) or an end stop, held either by U-bolt clips clamped over the doubled rope or by a soft metal sleeve crushed onto it with a crimping tool, so the rope can be hooked, shackled or anchored without fraying or slipping.

title: Load-bearing stitch patterns for straps and webbing
description: A strap is overlapped on itself or round a buckle, ring or slot and sewn with a dense, planned stitch pattern (bar tacks, a box with an X, W shapes or close rows) so that the pull is shared by many stitches and the joint can carry a large share of the webbing's own strength.

title: Hitches to a post, rail, ring or eye
description: A knot that ties a line directly to a post, rail, ring, bar, eye, log or a hole in a part, holding by the turns and tucks gripping the object and the rope itself, so it needs no hardware or tools and can be untied by hand; which hitch to use depends on what you tie to and whether you will adjust or release it.

title: Tensioning and adjustable hitches
description: Knots that tension a line and hold it with no hardware: the trucker's hitch ties a loop into the rope that works like a pulley so you can haul a lashing tight, while friction hitches such as the taut-line, rolling, adjustable grip and Prusik hitches wrap round a rope or pole, grip when the line is loaded and slide by hand when it is slack, so the line can be tightened or moved again later.

title: Eyelets and grommets
description: A small metal or plastic ring set into a punched hole in fabric, leather or thin sheet, with its tube (barrel) rolled over onto a washer or onto the material itself, so the hole has a smooth, strong rim that a lace, cord, hook, peg or pole can pass through without tearing the material.

title: Bead-in-groove fabric edge
description: A thick bead along the edge of a fabric, either sewn or welded in (keder, bolt rope, silicone edge strip) or pressed in over the fabric as a separate cord (screen spline), sits in a groove whose mouth is narrower than the bead, so the fabric edge is held, tensioned and often sealed along its whole length without a fastener at every point.

title: Fixed loop knots
description: Knots that make a loop that won't shrink or slip, at the end of a rope (bowline, figure-eight loop) or in its middle (alpine butterfly), to hook, clip or drop over something, and that untie by hand afterwards.

title: Bends for joining two cords
description: Knots that join two cords end to end, or close one cord into a ring: the sheet bend for cords of different thickness, the double fisherman's for a compact, very secure join, the water knot for flat tape, and the Zeppelin bend when it must still untie after a heavy pull.

title: Pole lashings
description: Rope wrapped round poles where they cross or touch and then tightened with turns between them, to make rigid frames, braced crossings, scissor legs, tripods and lengthened poles with no hardware or cut joints.

title: Rope-end finishing
description: A finish put on the cut end of a rope, cord or strap (tight turns of twine, melted fibres, strands tucked back, tape, a rubbery dip or a small cap) that holds the fibres together so the end does not fray, and often makes it easier to thread through holes.

title: Sewn seams and hand stitches
description: Two pieces of fabric or leather are held together by a line of thread stitched through both, by machine (usually a lockstitch) or by hand (running, back or saddle stitch), with the cut edges folded in, wrapped or overstitched so they can't fray.

title: Lacing
description: A lace is threaded back and forth through matching holes, eyelets or hooks on two edges and pulled tight, so many short crossings share the pull and draw the edges together; a knot, bow or lace lock holds it, and it can be loosened and re-tightened at any time.

title: Rope splices
description: A rope splice opens up the end of a rope and weaves its strands over and under the strands of the main rope, or, in hollow braided rope, pulls the end up inside the rope, to make a permanent loop, a join between two ropes or a neat end that keeps most or all of the rope's strength, where a knot typically loses 20-40% (Wikipedia 'Rope splicing').

title: Leather and textile rivets
description: A small two-part or hollow metal rivet pushed through a punched hole in leather, webbing or fabric and squashed with a setter against a hard anvil, so its two heads clamp the layers together permanently to fix straps, handles, tabs and buckles or to reinforce the corners of pockets and seams.

title: Chicago screw
description: A Chicago screw is a hollow post with a thread inside and a matching screw that threads into it from the other side, clamping leather, straps, paper, plastic or printed parts between two smooth, low heads like a rivet, but one that can be unscrewed to swap a buckle or used as a pivot pin.

title: Iron-on fusible web
description: A thin, dry web or film of hot-melt glue, sold as sheets, tape or already on the back of interfacing and patches, that is laid between fabrics and pressed with an iron so it melts into both and sets as it cools, giving a no-sew hem, appliqué or patch.

title: Binding knots and seizings
description: A group of knots and wrappings that squeeze round something to hold it together: the constrictor knot grips a bundle, bag neck or hose so hard it may have to be cut off, a seizing binds two ropes side by side with many turns of small twine, and cable lacing ties wire bundles into a neat loom with a row of locked stitches.

title: Tripod and stand screw mount
description: A single standard threaded socket or stud, nearly always 1/4-20 or 3/8-16 UNC, that lets any camera, light, phone holder or home-made part be screwed by hand onto any tripod, stand or rig, with locating pins, a lip, a rubber pad or a lock ring added because one screw on its own lets the part twist.

title: Clamp-on accessory mount for bars, poles and edges
description: A clamp that grips an existing bar, pole, tube, pipe or desk edge by squeezing it, often through a rubber pad, so an accessory can be fixed on, repositioned or removed without drilling or changing the thing it is clamped to.

title: Slotted adjustment with a jacking screw
description: A part is fixed with screws through slots instead of round holes, so it can be slid to set a belt or chain tension or line it up, usually pushed by a separate adjusting (jacking) screw, and is then locked by tightening the screws.

title: Castor
description: An unpowered wheel in a fixed or swivelling bracket fixed under an object so it can be rolled; a swivel castor's wheel trails behind its pivot so it lines itself up with the direction of travel, and braked versions lock the wheel, the swivel or both.

title: Levelling foot
description: A threaded stud with a foot pad that screws into the bottom of a leg, cabinet or machine; turning it in or out raises or lowers that corner so the piece stands steady and level, and the ball joint under many pads lets the pad lie flat on a sloping or uneven floor.

title: Spring clip clamp
description: Two jaws joined by a pivot and closed by a spring (usually a coiled wire torsion spring, sometimes rubber bands or a springy printed arm), so you squeeze the handles to open it and let go to clamp it onto cloth, paper, a board edge, a rod or a cable.

title: In-line swivel
description: A link with an eye at each end, joined through a body by a shaft that turns freely, so twist that builds up in a fishing line, lead, rope or chain can unwind instead of kinking or tangling, while the swivel still carries the pull.

title: Multi-point bolt
description: A multi-point bolt ties two or more bolts to one handle, through a turning rod with hooked or cam ends or a small gear driving toothed bars, so a single movement locks a tall door, a pair of doors or a big lid at the top, the bottom and sometimes the sides.

title: Flywheel
description: A flywheel is a heavy wheel on a shaft that stores energy as spin, so it evens out jerky turning, carries a crank past the points where it can't be pushed round, and keeps a machine or toy going for a while after the push stops.

title: Spot weld
